intro: How each roof's estimate is made, from the data sources to the money. Tap a step for more, and Details for the figures and the code behind them.

steps.title: Build the 3D landscape
steps.summary: Building outlines, a laser scan of every roof and tree, and aerial photos, all from LINZ.

items.title: Which buildings exist
items.text: Every building outline in an area comes from LINZ's NZ Building Outlines, picked by the suburb, town and council LINZ records on each outline.

items.title: A laser scan of the roofs
items.text: LINZ's LiDAR survey for the area: the raw point cloud (from OpenTopography's copy) where it has been published, and LINZ's surface model otherwise. Only points classed as building are used for roofs. The ground model and surface model give trees, neighbours and hills.

items.title: Distant hills
items.text: LINZ's national elevation model, out past the area, for hills on the horizon.

items.title: Aerial photos
items.text: LINZ aerial photos, the newest that cover the area, for roof lines and objects on roofs. The map itself shows LINZ Basemaps' photo.

items.title: Places with no laser scan
items.text: Where no LiDAR survey exists, roofs are modelled from the outline: a gable or hipped roof at 20° for houses and flat for large buildings. Every such building says so on the map.

items.title: Lining the data up
items.text: The photo and the scan were taken in different years and lean differently. Each roof's lean is measured by matching the photos (up to 4 m), and an outline that sits off the scanned roof is slid onto it (up to 2 m) without changing its shape.

steps.title: Read each roof
steps.summary: Find the roof's faces, their slope and direction, and anything on them.

items.title: Four readings of the roof
items.text: Each roof is read four ways: an image model that outlines shapes in the photo, a model trained on hand-drawn roof lines, the laser scan's flat regions, and the simplest roof form that fits. Each reading is scored on how well its edges match the lines in the photo and how well its faces fit the scan, and the best is kept.

items.title: When the reading is doubtful
items.text: A reading scoring under 0.30 is not used. One under 0.60 competes with faces found from the laser scan alone, and the scan's version wins when it explains the roof better or more simply.

items.title: Hand-drawn roofs come first
items.text: Where a person has drawn a roof's faces and lines, the drawing is used as it is. Identical roofs in a row of houses share the reading that explains the whole set best.

items.title: Slope and direction
items.text: Each face gets a flat plane fitted to its laser points, ignoring points more than 30 cm off it. Faces steeper than 55° are walls, not roof. A roof whose points fit its planes less than 45% of the time gets no panels.

items.title: Objects on the roof
items.text: Vents, skylights, chimneys and plant are found two ways: laser points standing more than 0.4 m off the roof's plane, and patches of the photo that stand out from the roof around them (within 1.2 m). Panels keep clear of both.

steps.title: Sunlight
steps.summary: How much sun reaches a roof of each slope and direction over a year.

items.title: Clear-sky sun, hour by hour
items.text: The sun's path and clear-sky light for every hour of a year, from the pvlib library's Ineichen model.

items.title: Cloud, from measured records
items.text: Each month is scaled to measured sunlight: NIWA's SolarView record for Queenstown where it applies, else the nearest NIWA radiation station (within 1.5°). Differences across the area come from the ERA5 climate record, held between 0.85 and 1.15 of the measured figure.

items.title: Onto a sloped roof
items.text: Sunlight is split into direct and diffuse light (the Erbs method) and turned onto each roof slope and direction with the Perez sky model, in 5° slope by 10° direction steps.

steps.title: Shade
steps.summary: Hills, trees and buildings that block the sun, worked out for every panel.

items.title: Nearby trees and buildings
items.text: From each panel, the laser scan's surface is searched in every direction (every 4°, out to 100 m) for anything that blocks the sun.

items.title: Hills
items.text: Each building's horizon of hills, in 72 directions out to 20 km, seen from its eaves, and the area's own horizon out to 30 km.

items.title: Deep shade
items.text: Direct sun that is blocked is taken off; light from the open sky is reduced by how much sky the panel sees. A panel keeping less than 45% of its direct sun is not placed.

steps.title: Panels and power
steps.summary: Lay panels sunniest first and work out what each one makes.

items.title: Laying out panels
items.text: 500 W panels (1.134 × 1.961 m) are packed in rows on each face, 0.10 m from edges and ridges, portrait unless landscape fits 40% more. A face pointing away from the sun with less than 78% of the sunniest face's sun is left bare. Stray panels go: an array needs at least 3.

items.title: Sunniest first
items.text: Panels are ranked by how much they make, so a smaller system takes the best spots. The density slider fills in that order.

items.title: Power from each panel
items.text: Each panel's sunlight after shade, times its rating, less 16.4% for the inverter, heat, dirt, wiring and glass reflection. The building's total is the sum of its panels.

items.title: Buildings that are gone
items.text: An outline whose building no longer shows in the newest photo is withheld.

items.title: Heat map mode
items.text: The heat map colours every 0.4 m of roof by its yearly sunlight, from the same sun and shade model.

steps.title: Money
steps.summary: Bills before and after, the cost, and the saving once a loan is repaid.

items.title: A household's day
items.text: Each building's use of power hour by hour, for an average day in each season: a home from the Electricity Authority's figures for its area, scaled for people and house size; a business by its floor area. Solar powers the building first; the rest is exported.

items.title: Batteries
items.text: A battery charges only from spare solar. On a time-of-use plan it saves its charge for peak hours, giving off-peak only what the coming peak will not need before the sun refills it; on a flat plan it covers any shortfall as it comes. Each season's typical day is repeated until the battery's charge settles, and the charts show it charging and powering the home.

items.title: Power prices
items.text: Home prices are the Electricity Authority's latest for Queenstown (Aurora Energy) (2026-05): 33.55c a kWh and $2.02 a day for a standard-use home, incl. GST. The one price is split into 52c in peak hours and 26c off-peak, so a typical home pays about the same average. Areas on another network use its prices: Central Otago (Aurora Energy) 40.69c and $1.99 a day; Southland (The Power Company) 31.28c and $3.38 a day. Exported solar earns 12c a kWh in the first year (retailer buy-back rates on Powerswitch). The prices are refreshed each month.

items.title: Cost and savings
items.text: The cost per kW falls with system size (Assumptions & pricing). Over a 30-year life power prices rise 4.0% a year, export rates fall 2.0% a year and panels lose 0.5% a year, shown in today's dollars.

items.title: Net saving with a loan
items.text: The green box: bill savings less the repayments on a loan for the system and its one replacement inverter, at 5.5% over 30 years. Both can be changed.

steps.title: Checks and publishing
steps.summary: Every figure is re-worked and checked before it reaches the map.

items.title: Every figure shows its workings
items.text: Tap a number on a building's card to see the sum that made it. The map re-works every panel's power from the published inputs and refuses to publish on any mismatch.
